text: Every woman knows a woman who's been raped, but no man ever knows a rapist. And that is something that really hits home because it really shows how much men turn a blind eye. If you're not honest about the messiness, it's just going to be sweat plunging around and people are going to suffer. Every woman knows a woman who's been RAPed, but no man ever knows an RAPist. This video went viral about a month ago, and as usual, it created very polarized opinions online. Many women jumped straight to the conclusion that men actively protect other men who are RAPists, which is no wonder, since even the lady in the video says it really shows how much men turn a blind eye. And a lot of men said, look, we genuinely don't know an RAPist. Even if a guy RAPed someone, why would he tell us? But it still got me thinking, does the statement have any truth to it? And if yes, could there be another explanation besides, oh, it is men covering up for other men? Because if you think about it, there might be something behind the observation. Even as guys, I think many of us would agree that it isn't so uncommon to personally know a woman who mentioned SA or RAP happening to her. But it can be quite uncommon to personally know a guy whom you know RAPed someone. So how could those two things be true at the same time? I tried to do my own little investigation. It is by no means scientific research. There are many assumptions here, so don't treat it as the ultimate truth. Just me asking questions and trying to find more or less plausible answers. First, there seems to be a large mismatch between experiences reported in surveys and offenses known to police. The CDC's 2023-2024 survey estimated that 987,000 adult women experienced completed force penetration in the preceding 12 months. A separate US government estimate put the number of RAP offenses known to police in 2024 at 134,300. Those figures aren't directly comparable. One counts women, the other offenses, and the definitions and time periods don't match exactly. So this isn't an apples-to-apples comparison. But I think the survey data could be one of the closest national statistics you could find for exploring a woman knowing another woman who was RAPed, while recorded RAP offenses could be one of the closest for exploring a man knowing an RAPist. Neither directly measures what friends know, but it does show that many experiences described in surveys may never appear in police records. Now, why we have that gap is an interesting but separate question. But there does seem to be a substantial difference between the two estimates, and numerically, one is more than seven times larger than the other. Second, could friendship and talking about personal things play a role? Pew survey found women more often said they discussed mental health with close friends, 31% versus 15% of men. Another Pew survey found women more often said they turned to a friend for emotional support, 54% versus 38%. These aren't RAP disclosure rates, but they do suggest personal experiences might circulate differently in women's and men's social circles. And the third reason is the one mentioned at the beginning. A survivor may tell friends what happened, while the person responsible may have reasons to hide it or downplay it. There is broader research showing that fear of judgment can discourage people from sharing negative information about themselves, and that people responsible for hurting someone may minimize what they did when describing it. That doesn't give us a disclosure rate for RAPists, but I think it makes this a plausible explanation. So, taken together, these three factors suggest it could be way more common to know a survivor than to know that someone is a perpetrator, without men protecting RAPists or turning a blind eye. That doesn't mean nobody does it. And when someone knowingly protects an RAPist, condemn them, criticize them. I'm sure most men would have no problem with that, but also understand that a gap in what people hear is not enough to establish that men generally know and cover for them.
